title: Larkin Traded to Canadiens for Dach, Hage in Major Red Wings Package Deal【NHL.com】
body:
Detroit’s rebuilding engine roared to life on Tuesday as the Red Wings sent forward Tyler Larkin to the Montreal Canadiens in a multi‑asset deal that also shuttles goaltender Samuel Montembeault and a quartet of draft selections to Detroit. In return, Montreal receives Larkin along with a package centered on forward Noah Dach and defenseman Jérémy Hage, while the Wings secure a promising young netminder and valuable future picks, underscoring Detroit’s commitment to a long‑term overhaul.

The trade marks a dramatic pivot for both clubs. Larkin, a gritty 27‑year‑old who was serving a two‑game suspension for an on‑ice incident, had struggled to find a consistent role in Detroit’s bottom‑six forward group this season. His departure clears cap space and opens a roster spot for emerging talent. Montreal, meanwhile, adds a player known for his physicality and penalty‑killing acumen, hoping the veteran presence will bolster a Canadiens roster that has flirted with the playoff bubble but lacks depth down the middle. The inclusion of Dach—a 25‑year‑old who posted eight points (two goals, six assists) in 22 games for the Habs—provides a modest offensive lift, while Hage offers a versatile defensive option capable of contributing on the power play.

For Detroit, the centerpiece of the return is Samuel Montembeault, a 26‑year‑old goaltender who posted a 2.45 goals‑against average and a .913 save percentage over 38 games this season. Montembeault’s steady performance in the net has made him a coveted asset for a team desperate to stabilize its last line of defense. Coupled with four draft picks—two second‑rounders, a third‑rounder, and a conditional seventh—Detroit positions itself to stockpile young talent and potentially flip those selections in future trades. General manager Steve Yzerman, who has overseen a steady stream of roster turnover, indicated that the move aligns with a broader strategy to accumulate assets while the team remains out of contention.

Analysts note that the trade reflects divergent timelines. Montreal, still aiming for a postseason push, is willing to part with future assets to acquire immediate help. The Canadiens have struggled to generate consistent secondary scoring, and Larkin’s proven ability to win face‑offs and deliver gritty minutes could be the missing piece in tight games. Moreover, his experience in high‑pressure situations may prove valuable as the Habs fight for a wild‑card berth in the Eastern Conference. Conversely, Detroit’s emphasis on draft capital signals a patient rebuild. By securing additional second‑round picks, the Wings increase their odds of landing a top‑tier prospect, while the conditional seventh‑rounder could become a hidden gem if the team scouts wisely.

The trade also has salary‑cap implications. Larkin’s one‑year, $3.6 million contract, signed on July 16, 2026, fits comfortably under Montreal’s cap ceiling, allowing the Habs to retain flexibility for potential free‑agent signings. Detroit, shedding Larkin’s salary, frees up space to either re‑sign emerging players or explore additional acquisitions. Montembeault’s contract, at $3.3 million for the upcoming season, is a modest commitment for a goalie who could evolve into a starter, further sweetening the deal for Detroit’s front office.

Looking ahead, the true impact of this transaction will unfold over the next few months. Montreal will gauge Larkin’s integration into their bottom six and assess whether his presence translates into improved special‑teams performance and grit in close contests. Detroit, meanwhile, will monitor Montembeault’s adaptation to a new defensive system and evaluate the draft picks as the 2027 NHL Entry Draft approaches. Both organizations have taken calculated risks, balancing present needs against future aspirations, and the ripple effects of this trade could shape the competitive landscape of the league well into the next season.
